summary: The note argues that increasingly frequent and intense natural disasters are exposing weaknesses in power grids, and calls for investment in resilience. It describes a 2023 hurricane in Florida, an earthquake in Japan, and floods in Bengal, India, with personal accounts of prolonged outages. It closes with expert recommendations for a smarter, decentralized grid and a call for governments, utilities and communities to act.
one_line: Hurricane, earthquake and flood case studies from Florida, Japan and India show power grid vulnerability and the need for resilient, smart grid investment.
key_facts: Hurricane Elara made landfall on Florida's southern coast on October 14, 2023, as a Category 4 storm with winds of 130 mph.
Hurricane Elara snapped electricity poles and submerged entire substations, disrupting millions of Floridians within hours.
Jonathan McAllister of Tallahassee endured a power outage lasting nearly three weeks, with spoiled food and downed cell networks.
Maria Gonzales' small bakery in Florida could not serve customers because its ovens were cold without electricity.
A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck Japan on September 8, 2023, collapsing power lines and causing fires at transformer stations.
The September 8, 2023 Japan earthquake left over 2 million households in Tokyo without electricity for more than a day.
Takashi Kobayashi, a Tokyo-based civil engineer, says each new seismic event poses new challenges even though Japan has invested heavily in earthquake-resistant infrastructure.
Floods struck Bengal, India, on November 13, 2023, submerging power stations and causing outages that lasted over one month.
Anika Patel, a local energy official, said floodwaters damaged high-voltage equipment that will take months to repair or replace.
Linda Robinson's family in Florida drained their pool to flush toilets and cooked leftover food on a barbecue during the outage.
Dr. Helen Price, a UK electrical infrastructure specialist, advocates a 'grid of the future' combining sturdy physical structures with smart technology.
Dr. Price suggests advanced warning systems, decentralized energy sources such as solar and battery storage, automated response and rapid recovery mechanisms.
Power failures stop water purification, overburden emergency services and disable communications, affecting life-or-death situations.
The note says investments in grid preparedness cost far less than post-disaster recovery in economic terms and human lives.
